Effective Nov. 1, 2025, the camping limit at Mittry Lake will change from 10 days per calendar year to 14 days within a 28-day period . This update aligns Mittry Lake with surrounding BLM-managed public lands and improves consistency in enforcement among the coordinating agencies. Visitors may camp up to 14 days within any 28-day period at Mittry Lake. After 14 days, campers must move to another site at least 25 miles away. All other recreation rules remain unchanged. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn BLM Turns Wildfire Response into Opportunity for Forest Management and Local Industry Aug 21, 2026 Montrose, Colo. – A firebreak along Cimarron Road during the Gold Mountain Fire served another purpose, too: putting removed trees to use. When wildfire conditions make direct suppression difficult or unsafe, firefighters look for places where they can use the landscape to slow a fire's spread. Reducing vegetation along roads can create a break in fuels, giving firefighters another option if conditions change. That approach was used along nearly 2 miles of Cimarron Road northeast of Ridgway. Crews removed vegetation within approximately 75 feet of the roadside to create a potential firebreak if the fire moved in that direction. Before the work began, Ken Smothers, forester with the BLM's Gunnison Field Office, completed an expedited timber cruise to identify trees that could be recovered and sold rather than left as waste. Share sensitive information only on official, secure websites. https://www.nist.gov/blockchain Information technology Blockchain Sign Up to Get NIST News GovDelivery Blockchain technology provides a way for a community of participants to maintain a shared, tamper-evident, and tamper-resistant digital ledger. It is the underlying technology for many cryptocurrency systems, but it can also be used in other types of applications. A blockchain is the ledger itself. It contains transactional records that are grouped into blocks. Each block is cryptographically linked to the previous block, making the ledger tamper evident. If data in an earlier block is changed, the cryptographic link to that block changes, and the change can be detected in later blocks. As new blocks are added, older blocks become more difficult to modify, creating tamper resistance. A blockchain network is the network in which a blockchain is used. Copies of the ledger are maintained across nodes in the network, and new blocks are added according to established validation and consensus rules. This distributed structure, together with cryptographic mechanisms, helps make the blockchain resilient to later attempts to alter the ledger. pages.text: Bobby Thomson's Scottish family reacts on his home run's 75th anniversary Skip to Content Design by Tom Forget It was called “The shot heard ‘round the world” – though the newspaper editors who coined it likely had no idea how right they were. While American baseball has never been shy about applying a global moniker to its domestic contests (it is called the World Series after all), Bobby Thomson’s iconic pennant-winning home run against the Brooklyn Dodgers on Oct. 3, 1951 really did deserve the globe-spanning moniker. These games were among the first to receive nationwide broadcast on television and radio, with the call also going out to U.S. service members around the world thanks to Armed Forces Radio. And then there was Thomson, who was originally born in a two-room tenement building in Glasgow, becoming known in the States as “The Staten Island Scot.” But what was the reaction back in Thomson’s homeland of Scotland? ​ “Every once in a while, you do come across somebody who's aware of Bobby Thomson, but I wouldn't say it's in everyday Scottish sports folklore,” John Tafe, an American ex-pat and the current president of Baseball Scotland, told MLB.com. “He's not on the pantheon of Scottish heroes or anything like that. Search Twitter YouTube Facebook Instagram Flickr LinkedIn Boise District Office The Boise District, located in southwest Idaho, manages approximately 4 million acres of public land stretching from the central Idaho mountains to the borders with Oregon and Nevada. The District has many challenges to face as it balances its mission of multiple use and sustainable yield to achieve a sustainable ecosystem. Some of the major activities occurring within the district include: livestock grazing, wildland fire suppression, as well as motorized and non-motorized recreation. The Boise District is divided into three geographic areas/field offices: Bruneau (1.4 million acres), Four Rivers (1.3 million acres) and Owyhee (1.2 million acres). The District also manages Idaho's only National Conservation Area, Morley Nelson Snake River Birds of Prey (487,000 acres), home to the greatest concentration of nesting birds of prey in North America – and perhaps, the world. Some 800 pairs of hawks, owls, eagles and falcons come each spring to mate and raise their young here. pages.description: Rapper Bad Bunny may have shone a light on Puerto Rico’s cultural riches recently, but the Caribbean island has long been a place of bounty — with seas that glow in the dark, beaches that hide pirate loot and sacred mountains that burst with flora.
pages.text: Bomba and bioluminescence—Puerto Rico is full of surprises | National Geographic By Amanda Canning Last updated December 17, 2025 This article was produced by National Geographic Traveller (UK). The inhabitants of San Juan aren’t early risers. At 9am, the city’s streets are largely empty. In the Plaza Colón, there’s a cockerel scrabbling about in the flower beds. A kiosk selling coffee and empanadas is untroubled by customers. “We like a slow start,” Laura Ortiz-Villamil confirms as we sit in the shade, the sun already blazing. In front of us is a statue of Christopher Columbus, a crucifix raised in his left hand. Among the first Europeans to barrel over the Atlantic, all eager to get their hands on whatever land they could, he ‘discovered’ Puerto Rico in 1493 and immediately claimed it for Spain. “The Spanish called it Puerto Rico — rich port — wrongly believing there was gold here,” Laura says as we set off on a stroll around the capital’s historic district, Old San Juan. A born-and-bred Puerto Rican, with tattoos on her arms ranging from Gabriel García Márquez quotes to Peanuts characters, historian Laura set up her guiding company in 2022 to share her country’s “less-known stories, good or bad”. We wander cobbled streets flanked by houses with arched wooden doorways and overhanging balconies, painted in every colour you might think of: pistachio, peach, lemon, spearmint. Some are in a state of beautiful decay, untouched for centuries; others are as spick and span as if the decorators only just moved out. The salt flats are about 12 miles long and 5 miles wide and are comprised mostly of sodium chloride, or table salt. Located 120 miles west of Salt Lake City in Tooele County, Utah, the salt flats are a 30,000 acre expanse of hard, white salt crust on the western edge of the Great Salt Lake Basin in Utah. Like the Great Salt Lake, the Salt Flats are a remnant of Lake Bonneville, which covered over one-third of Utah from 10,000 to 32,000 years ago. The salt flats are on the National Register of Historic Places, are designated as an Area of Critical Environmental Concern, and are managed as a Special Recreation Management Area. The salt flats are generally open to the public for recreational purposes. Motor vehicle use is limited by seasonal closure during the spring when the salt is moist or has standing water on the surface. Closure dates may vary and will be posted by sign.
